chapters.title: The Two Rivals
comprehension_flags: "The preachers of the islands" — "islands" (jazāʾir) was the Ismaili mission's technical term for its regional administrative jurisdictions; a modern reader unfamiliar with this usage may take the word geographically and miss that Syria, Iran, and Yemen are being named as three such regions.

chapters.title: The Judge and His Cosmos
comprehension_flags: The paragraph describing al-Kirmani's cosmological framework — the Active Intellect, Universal Soul, ten Platonic intellects, and the nested worlds from origination down to religion — uses terms without gloss that a non-specialist reader is unlikely to follow, but adding explanation here would exceed this pass's authorization.
terminology_notes: "al-tatil" is rendered "invalidity" in the source; the Arabic theological literature more commonly glosses it as "divesting" or "stripping" (God of attributes) — worth confirming the book-wide rendering before this chapter goes to final.

chapters.title: The Perfect and Perfection
editorial_queries: Section 1, al-Nusra's opening statement — "he does not recognize that perfection is better and more complete than the perfect" — the reasoning that immediately follows establishes the perfect (bearer, what is described) as superior to perfection (attribute, borne), which suggests the intended order of the two terms may be reversed in this sentence.

Section 2's closing principle — "that existence by which it exists is below it in nobility and precedence" — is rendered to mean the effect (the perfect) is below its cause (perfection), which the argument requires; the surface grammar may suggest the reverse, and the Arabic source would resolve the question.
comprehension_flags: "the Following one," "the Preceding one," "the Asas," "the Speaker," and "the Limit" are Ismaili cosmological ranks used without gloss throughout; a modern reader unfamiliar with this hierarchy will find several passages in Sections 7 and 8 difficult to follow.

Section 7's phrase "even if there be in it a god" — "it" refers to the Limit (a specific rank), and the statement turns on an Ismaili theological distinction between the Limit's self-knowledge and the divine itself, which is not explained in the passage.

chapters.title: Nothing Stands Beside the First
comprehension_flags: The chapter ends mid-sentence ("since there is not") — this is deliberate, as the argument continues in the next section; a reader may assume it is a transcription error rather than an intentional stopping point.
terminology_notes: "the Following" — technical name for the Soul as the second emanation, used as a proper noun throughout; ensure spelling is standardized across the book.
"the Word" — used as an alternative name for the First Intellect; ensure consistency with the book's established usage elsewhere.

chapters.title: The Soul That Forgets
editorial_queries: In Chapter Twenty-One, "the First, and the author of al-Islah, all said" names two parties but uses "all," which may indicate a third authority is implied or that the phrasing is an artifact of the source's formulation.

The heading "Chapter Thirty-Seven of Part One" appears twice in sequence — once for a shorter version of the exchange and once for an extended version concluded by "We say:" — which may reflect a deliberate structural feature of the source or a textual duplication; the passage has been rendered exactly as given.
comprehension_flags: "The upper letters" in the abode of origination is a technical term in this philosophical system referring to cosmological entities; a reader without grounding in Ismaili cosmology will not know what "letters" designates here.

The phrase "the horizons and the souls" functions as a technical criterion of doctrinal reliability with a Quranic resonance (41:53) that a general reader unfamiliar with the tradition will not recognize.
terminology_notes: "the Follower" — should be confirmed as the consistent book-wide rendering for this figure in the cosmological hierarchy, as the source capitalizes it and uses it as a proper term.

chapters.title: Motion, Stillness, and the Bodiless Intellect
editorial_queries: In Chapter Two, the chapter heading attributes the whole passage to "the author of al-Islah," but the phrase "contrary to what he mentioned" refers to al-Islah in the third person, suggesting the narrator's commentary begins at "This is a picture that may not be held as a literal belief" — the boundary of the direct quotation is unclear.

chapters.title: Light, Darkness, and the Matter Below
The Fruit of Two Worlds
comprehension_flags: In the opponent's rebuttal in the second section, the phrase "would not let him return to these persons, so that he should forget" is elliptical — "these persons" appears to refer to embodied human beings in the world, but the referent is unstated, and the causal link between that return and the forgetting may stop a modern reader.

chapters.title: Body, Form, and the Two Letters of 'Be'
The Small World
comprehension_flags: "jewels" is used as a technical term for fundamental categories or classes of being — an unusual usage that may stop a modern reader on first encounter.
terminology_notes: "knotted" (First Section, in the voice of al-Islah) and "contracted" (Fifth Section onward, in the voice of al-Nusrah and in the subsequent analysis) appear to be the same technical term rendered two different ways; a single consistent English choice should be applied to both throughout the book.

chapters.title: Fleeing to God's Measure
comprehension_flags: "al-Jadd" is used throughout as a named cosmic figure without definition in this passage; a reader new to the book's technical hierarchy will not know what he is or his place among the Preceder, Follower, Speaker, and Foundation.
"the master of the affair" in the Moses section refers to Shuayb (ع), but the identification is given only mid-passage; the antecedent is unclear on first reading before the gloss appears.

chapters.title: Did Adam Bring a Law?
comprehension_flags: "In the Hereafter and in the beginning" — the phrase "the beginning" (mabda') is a technical Ismaili theological term for the primordial origin of existence, paired with "the return" (ma'ad, rendered here as "the Hereafter"); a modern reader may take "in the beginning" as a temporal reference rather than a cosmological one, which would invert its meaning.

"the Speakers" is a specialist term for prophets who proclaimed a formal Law and strove in its cause; modern readers may also stumble on "possessors of firm resolve," which refers to the five major prophets — Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad — recognized in the Quran as those who bore especially demanding missions; both terms may benefit from a gloss elsewhere in the book.
terminology_notes: rite-keeper — the term for one devoted to the rite (mansak); confirm this rendering is consistent wherever the same Arabic concept recurs in the book.
private parts — this phrase renders a specific Islamic legal category (the domain the Law protects in matters of chastity and lineage); its rendering should be confirmed and standardized book-wide.

chapters.title: The Six Gates of Necessity
editorial_queries: "their claiming for Him what Allah did not place in him" — the antecedents conflict: "Him" (capitalized, apparently referring to Allah) and "him" (lowercase, apparently referring to creation or Adam), leaving unclear whether creation makes false theological claims about God or false claims about their own endowments.
terminology_notes: speaker-prophets — this is a specialized technical term (likely rendering Arabic nutaqa') and its spelling and hyphenation should be standardized throughout the book.

chapters.title: Creativity Is the Creator
comprehension_flags: "the two acts of worship" in the concluding section is left unnamed; a modern reader unfamiliar with the Ismaili tradition may not know what these two practices are, since the text describes their observance in detail but does not state them.
